tagline: Boot-shaped home of Rome and the Renaissance
overview:
Italy is easy to spot on any map: a long boot kicking the island of Sicily across the Mediterranean Sea. The country is about the size of Arizona and stretches from the snowy Alps in the north down a spine of mountains to sun-baked southern shores. Its capital, Rome, was the center of an empire 2,000 years ago, and ancient ruins stand next to Renaissance palaces and modern scooters. Venice floats on canals, Florence is a museum of art, Milan is a fashion and business capital, and Naples sits beneath the volcano Vesuvius.

About 59 million people live in Italy and speak Italian, with many regional dialects and a few German- and French-speaking valleys in the north. Italy is a parliamentary republic and a founding member of the European Union. It has the most UNESCO World Heritage Sites of any country, and its food, from pizza and pasta to gelato and espresso, is eaten in every corner of the world. Two tiny independent states, Vatican City and San Marino, sit inside its borders.
landAndNature: The Alps form Italy's northern wall, with Monte Bianco, shared with France, the highest point at 4,808 meters, and the pale jagged Dolomites glowing pink at sunset. Below them the fertile Po Valley is Italy's farm belt and industrial heartland. The Apennine Mountains run the length of the peninsula. Italy is one of Europe's most volcanic countries: Mount Etna on Sicily is the tallest active volcano in Europe, Stromboli erupts almost constantly, and Vesuvius buried Pompeii in AD 79. Lakes Como, Garda, and Maggiore lie at the foot of the Alps. The coasts range from the cliffs of Amalfi to the beaches of Sardinia. Wolves and brown bears live in the Apennines, Alpine ibex in the north, and olive groves and vineyards cover the hills.
peopleAndCulture: Italian life revolves around family and food. Each region has its own dishes: pizza from Naples, pesto from Genoa, risotto from Milan, and hundreds of pasta shapes, followed by gelato or a tiny cup of espresso. Most Italians are Roman Catholic, and the Pope lives in Rome. Italy invented opera, and composers such as Verdi and Puccini fill theaters worldwide; Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Botticelli created masterpieces of the Renaissance. Soccer is a national obsession, and Italy has won the World Cup four times. Ferrari and Vespa were born here, and Milan sets fashion trends. Every evening people stroll through town centers in the passeggiata, and festivals like Venice's Carnival and Siena's bareback horse race, the Palio, keep old traditions alive.
history: Legend says Rome was founded in 753 BC by Romulus. The Roman Republic and then the Roman Empire ruled the Mediterranean world for centuries, spreading roads, Latin, and law before the western empire fell in 476. Italy broke into rival city-states such as Venice, Florence, and Genoa, which grew rich on trade and, in the 1300s and 1400s, launched the Renaissance, a rebirth of art and science. Foreign powers, including Spain, France, and Austria, controlled much of the peninsula for centuries. Italy was finally united as one kingdom in 1861, led by figures like Garibaldi. Benito Mussolini ruled as a fascist dictator from 1922 and joined Hitler in World War II; Italy became a republic in 1946 and helped found the European Union.
funFacts: Italy has 60 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, more than any other country in the world.
About 3,000 euros in coins are tossed into Rome's Trevi Fountain every day and donated to charity.
The University of Bologna, founded in 1088, is the oldest university in continuous operation in the world.
Italians eat about 23 kilograms of pasta per person each year, more than anyone else on Earth.
Italy has three active volcanoes, Etna, Stromboli, and Vesuvius, and Vesuvius is the only one on the European mainland to have erupted in the last century.
